extracted.intended_audience: poets, dramatists, and students of poetics (writers of tragedy, epic, and lyric verse)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing and evaluating poetic works (especially tragedy and epic): diction, metaphor, metre, unity of plot, scale, and appropriate use of the marvelous and improbable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perfection of style
rubrics_metrics.description: The perfection of style is to be clear without being mean.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A style composed only of common/proper words is clearest but 'mean'; unusual or rare words raise diction above the commonplace. The ideal mixes clarity (the ordinary) with elevation (rare/metaphorical/ornamental words) so as to be distinct yet perspicuous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance of common and rare words
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ a measured infusion of rare/strange words, metaphors, ornament, extensions, contractions, and alterations to raise diction above commonness while preserving clarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Too many rare/metaphorical terms makes a 'riddle' (if all metaphors) or 'jargon' (if all rare words). Use these devices to distinguish style, but not so wholly as to obscure sense; partial conformity with usage secures perspicuity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid wholly metaphorical or wholly rare diction
rubrics_metrics.description: A style made up entirely of metaphors is a riddle; entirely of rare words is a jargon; both are faults.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If all diction is metaphorical the poem becomes enigmatical; if all diction is strange it becomes unintelligible. Include some of these elements but not exclusively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderation in licentious devices (lengthening, extensions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Licenses of speech (lengthening syllables, extensions/contractions) must be used with moderation and not obtrusively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obtrusive lengthening or excessive alteration is grotesque and ludicrous: e.g. mock examples given by critics. Inserted ordinary forms or occasional licences are effective; continual abuse is ridiculed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of extension/contraction/alteration to gain distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: Extension, contraction, and alteration of words contribute to a clearness remote from commonness by providing distinction while retaining partial conformity with usage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These deviations should be exceptional to give distinction; they aid perspicuity by contrasting with normal idiom. Critics who condemn such licenses universally are incorrect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction appropriate to metre and genre
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose words and devices appropriate to the poetic measure and genre: compounds suit dithyrambs, rare words heroic poetry, metaphors iambic; conversational idiom suits iambic verse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different genres favor different word-types: heroic verse admits rare words and metaphors; iambic/imitative of familiar speech should favor common/proper/metaphorical/ornamental words. Use what fits the nature of the metre and genre.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genius for metaphor
rubrics_metrics.description: The greatest thing is to have a genius for metaphor; making good metaphors is a mark of a gifted nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Metaphor requires an eye for resemblances; it cannot be taught wholly by instruction. The capacity to make apt metaphors is the highest poetic faculty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of metaphor and correct formation
rubrics_metrics.description: Metaphor may be formed by transference: from genus to species, species to genus, species to species, or by analogy (proportion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples given (e.g. 'there stands my ship' as genus→species; numerical substitution as species→genus; analogy where the fourth term stands for the second). Metaphors can be qualified by mentioning the term to which the proper word is relative (e.g., 'shield of Dionysus').

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of newly-coined and altered words
rubrics_metrics.description: Poets may coin new words or alter words (extend, contract, or recast) for effect, but sparingly and with purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: New coinages (examples cited) can be effective; extension/ contraction give distinction (examples: πόλεως→adAnos, Πηλῆος) but must not be overused so as to render diction obscure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid barbarism or mixing excessive foreign/rare features
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not combine all exotic features at once: too many foreign dialects, metaphors, and rare words together yields either a riddle or barbarism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A mixture should be controlled: using many such features simultaneously may produce unintelligibility or mockery rather than elevated diction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity through proper nouns and partial conformity
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of proper/common names helps clearness; at the same time partial conformity with ordinary usage ensures perspicuity when employing exceptional diction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proper nouns give the firmest clarity; deviation in part from the idiom is effective because it contrasts with the expected, but retain enough of the ordinary to be understood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and function of word-types (simple/compound/double/etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Words may be simple (made of non-significant elements) or compound (composed of significant and non-significant elements or multiple significant elements); compounds can be triple, quadruple, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compound words and the variety of word-formation affect style and suit particular genres (magniloquent compounds for lofty diction). Understand these categories when choosing diction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sentence and unity of expression
rubrics_metrics.description: A sentence or phrase is a composite sound some parts of which are significant; unity can be by signifying one thing or by linking together parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A sentence may dispense with a verb and still be a unity; the notion of unity at sentence-level parallels unity at plot-level: the work should produce a single unified effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of plot (single action principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: A plot should be constructed on dramatic principles: it must have a single action, whole and complete, with a beginning, middle, and end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The single-action, organic structure produces the proper pleasure; avoid choosing a subject so vast or composite that it cannot be apprehended as a single complete action (Homer's selectivity praised).

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate scope and scale (length and manageability)
rubrics_metrics.description: The scale of a poem must permit the audience to embrace beginning and end in a single view; epic can be larger, tragedy is limited by stage presentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Epic may expand by narration of simultaneous events (adding mass/grandeur); tragedy must confine to what can be enacted by actors on stage without producing satiety through sameness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation of parts to whole (episodes and relevance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Episodes included in a larger poem must be relevant to the subject and contribute appropriately to the unity and variety of the poem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Epic may admit many episodes from the general story to diversify; but episodes should not destroy unity — they must serve the overall action or effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate use of metre
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose a metre fitting the imitation: heroic metre suits epic narrative; iambic and trochaic tetrameter suit action and dancing respectively; do not mix metres.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Heroic measure is stately and admits rare words/metaphor; iambic/trochaic measures are more kinetic. Experience (tradition) confirms the appropriateness of these metres for their functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of the wonderful and the irrational
rubrics_metrics.description: The marvelous (the wonderful) is permissible and pleasing but the irrational elements must not be such as reason decisively rejects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tragedy admits the wonderful to a degree; epic (not showing the actors) can more safely include the irrational. Avoid implausible incidents that would appear ludicrous on stage (e.g., pursuit of Hector staged with Greeks standing still). Conceal or render improbable-seeming elements plausible in diction and narrative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer probable impossibilities to improbable possibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet should prefer probable impossibilities (events that could not happen but are presented plausibly) to improbable possibilities (events that reason rejects).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tragic plots must avoid incidents the reason rejects; where the first element is untrue but the second true, audiences may infer the first—poets exploit such fallacies, but should do so carefully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poet's presence and showing vs telling
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet should speak as little as possible in person; he should introduce characters who immediately show distinctive ethical/behavioral traits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Homer is praised for bringing characters in who possess clear characteristics rather than the poet appearing frequently. Imitation is best done by presenting actions and characters rather than authorial explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization: each person must possess distinctive character
rubrics_metrics.description: When introducing a person, make them have characteristic qualities — no one should be wanting in distinctive manners or traits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characters must be credible and consistent; even in brief appearances they should show ethical traits that make them individuated and appropriate to the action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thought and diction must be artistic
rubrics_metrics.description: The thoughts (ideas, reasoning, thematic conception) and diction of the poem must be well crafted (artistic).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Homer is cited as a model who excelled both in diction and in thought. Reversals (peripeteia), recognitions (anagnorisis), and incidents must be handled artistically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of reversals, recognitions, and tragic incidents
rubrics_metrics.description: Both epic and tragedy require devices such as reversals of fortune, recognitions, and suffering (pathē) among their parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These elements are central to tragic effect and must be present (except song and scenery which differ); they serve the emotional and structural needs of the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid ludicrous improbabilities in the enacted drama
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not place on stage incidents that would seem ludicrous when enacted; what passes in narrative may fail when presented visually.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge content by how it would appear in performance: e.g., an onstage chase in which principals behave inconsistently will provoke laughter rather than wonder.
